learning_objective: 🎯 Enter the Middle Ages! Understand feudalism and how medieval European society was strictly divided into those who pray, those who fight, and those who work.

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Feudalism was a system based on land and loyalty. The King gave land (fiefs) to Lords. In return, Lords promised military service. The Lords then gave protection to peasants, who in return had to work the Lord's land.
'Those who pray'. The Catholic Church was immensely powerful and wealthy. It owned vast lands, had its own laws, and collected a tax called the 'Tithe' (one-tenth of the peasants' produce).
'Those who fight'. The nobles and knights held the real political and military power. They controlled large estates (manors) and held absolute authority over the peasants living on their lands.
'Those who work'. The majority of the population. 'Free peasants' paid rent, while 'Serfs' were bound to the lord's land, forced to labor for free, and could not leave without permission.

fun_activity.title: 🤝 The Vow of Vassalage
fun_activity.instructions: In medieval times, a Lord and Vassal sealed their contract with a ceremony. The Vassal would kneel, place his hands between the Lord's hands, and swear loyalty. Act out this dramatic 'Oath of Fealty' with a friend to understand medieval social bonds!

exam_tips: 📌 The 'Three Orders' refers to: Clergy, Nobility, and Peasantry. Know the specific roles and privileges (or lack thereof) of each.
📌 'Friars' were a new kind of monks who, unlike traditional monks isolated in abbeys, chose to live among the people and travel to preach.
📌 The 14th Century Crisis is a critical topic: The 'Black Death' (bubonic plague) wiped out a third of Europe, causing a massive labor shortage that weakened the feudal system.
quick_recap: ⭐ Medieval European society was structured around the exchange of land for military service and labor.
⭐ The Catholic Church held extraordinary independent power and wealth.
⭐ The strict social hierarchy began to crumble after the devastation of the Black Death in the 1300s.
